problem: Deep RL from raw pixels needs massive amounts of data and overfits to training environments, so policies transfer poorly to unseen buildings; existing representation-learning baselines (VAE, curiosity, dynamics, ImageNet) do not fix this.
motivation: Visual priors about the world (3D structure, semantics) should help downstream motor tasks. The authors observe that agents trained from scratch perform no better than a blind agent on unseen test buildings, suggesting they exploit spurious training-set biases instead of learning perception.
key_idea: Feed the RL policy the features of frozen, offline-trained mid-level vision networks (24 Taskonomy objectives such as depth, normals and object classification) instead of raw pixels, and pick a task-agnostic Max-Coverage set of features when the downstream task is unknown.
insight: Mid-level features make the train and test distributions look more alike. With 4 training buildings, scratch and curvature reach the same train reward, but test SPL is 0.65 for curvature vs 0.46 for scratch. Feature rankings are uncorrelated across tasks (Spearman ρ between -0.09 and 0.15): semantic features win at target navigation and geometric ones at exploration, so no single feature is universal. The Max-Coverage set of 4 features (0.749 SPL) nearly matches the best single feature (0.76), while the best task-agnostic single feature (autoencoder) drops to 0.58.
method: Frozen mid-level encoders: 24 ResNet-50 encoders from Taskonomy, trained offline on 4M real indoor images, map the RGB frame to a feature that is the policy's observation. Only the policy is trained.
Policy learning: off-policy PPO with a replay buffer, GAE advantages and a small controller network. Hyperparameters are tuned for scratch and reused for mid-level agents.

Baselines and controls: scratch (AtariNet), blind, random frozen projection, pixels-as-features, random actions, SLAM with estimated depth, and dynamics modeling, curiosity, DARLA and ImageNet features.
Tasks: local planning (PointNav), visual exploration, and visual-target navigation (a crate, sparse reward). Actions are turn ±10° and move 0.25 m, with no proprioception.

Max-Coverage feature set: a sequence of Boolean Integer Programs, binary-searched over the covering distance δ, on Taskonomy transfer affinities. It finds the smallest set of k features that minimizes worst-case distance to any ideal task feature.

Evaluation: 72 Gibson training buildings and 14 unseen test buildings, in Habitat, Gibson env and ViZDoom. Reported metrics are reward relative to blind, SPL, collisions and jerk, and rank-reversal significance tests.

setting.backbone: Frozen Taskonomy ResNet-50 mid-level encoders + small policy network trained with off-policy PPO (RL)
setting.training_data: Encoders: Taskonomy 4M static indoor images (frozen). Policy: RL in 72 Gibson training buildings (up to), tested on 14 unseen buildings
setting.observation: egocentric RGB plus minimal side info (target vector for PointNav, occupancy bitmap for exploration, past-location bitmap in Habitat); no proprioception
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: turn_left 10°, turn_right 10°, move_forward 0.25 m
setting.privileged: Ground-truth agent localization (IMU) is used in the main experiments; the noisy-localization ablation removes it

numbers_note: Most results are only in bar charts and figures. The benchmark is the authors' own Habitat/Gibson local-planning setup, not the official Habitat challenge test split. Exploration and visual-target navigation results are reported as reward, not as standard benchmark metrics.
results: Mid-level-vision agents reach 0.74-0.76 SPL on Habitat local planning, against under 0.57 SPL for scratch and the SotA representation baselines (curiosity 0.56). They also generalize better (0.65 vs 0.46 SPL with 4 training buildings), match scratch's final reward with 15% of the frames and with 8/72 buildings, and are more robust without ground-truth localization (0.73 vs 0.55 SPL for a map-using baseline).
limitations: Encoders are frozen and were not adapted to the RL task, which the authors acknowledge is 'almost certainly not ideal'.
Results are only in simulation on Gibson/Habitat/ViZDoom with three simple locomotion tasks; there is no language or semantic goal navigation and no real-robot experiments in the paper.
Feature choice depends on the task (rank reversal), and the Max-Coverage set relies on the Taskonomy affinity distance and only ties the best single feature.
